module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 89

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/89](https://www.erdosproblems.com/89)
- [Er46] Erdős, Paul. On sets of distances of $n$ points. Amer. Math. Monthly
  53 (1946), 248--250.
- [GuKa15] Guth, Larry and Katz, Nets Hawk. On the Erdős distinct distances
  problem in the plane. Ann. of Math. (2) 181 (2015), 155--190.
- [Mo52] Moser, Leo. On the different distances determined by $n$ points.
  Amer. Math. Monthly 59 (1952), 85--91.

### AI disclosure

Lean 4 code in this file was drafted with assistance from OpenAI Codex.
The mathematical content and references are the author's own work.
-/

@[expose] public section

open Filter
open EuclideanGeometry

namespace Erdos89

/--
Erdős [Er46] asked whether every set of $n$ distinct points in $\mathbb{R}^2$
determines $\gg \frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}$ many distinct distances.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 52]
theorem erdos_89 :
    (fun (n : ℕ) => n/(n : ℝ).log.sqrt) =O[atTop]
      (fun n => (minimalDistinctDistances ℝ² n : ℝ)) := by
  sorry

/--
Guth and Katz [GuKa15] proved that there are always $\gg \frac{n}{\log n}$
many distinct distances.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 52]
theorem erdos_89.variants.n_dvd_log_n :
    (fun (n : ℕ) => n/(n : ℝ).log) =O[atTop]
      (fun n => (minimalDistinctDistances ℝ² n : ℝ)) := by
  sorry

/--
The square grid construction, going back to Erdős and Moser, shows that
$\frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}$ is the correct order if the conjecture is true:
there are configurations whose number of distinct distances is
$O(\frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}})$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 52]
theorem erdos_89.variants.grid_upper_bound :
    (fun n => (minimalDistinctDistances ℝ² n : ℝ)) =O[atTop]
      (fun (n : ℕ) => n/(n : ℝ).log.sqrt) := by
  sorry

/--
This theorem provides a sanity check, showing that the main conjecture (`erdos_89`) is strictly
stronger than the solved Guth and Katz result. It proves that, trivially, if the lower bound
$\frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}$ holds, then the weaker lower bound $\frac{n}{\log n}$ must also hold.
-/
@[category test, AMS 52]
theorem erdos_89.variants.implies_n_dvd_log_n (h : type_of% erdos_89) :
    type_of% erdos_89.variants.n_dvd_log_n := by
  refine .trans ?_ h
  have := (Asymptotics.isLittleO_one_left_iff ℝ).mpr <| tendsto_norm_atTop_atTop.comp <|
    (tendsto_rpow_atTop (show 0 < 1/2 by norm_num)).comp
    (Real.tendsto_log_atTop.comp tendsto_natCast_atTop_atTop)
  convert! (Asymptotics.isBigO_refl (fun n : ℕ ↦ n/(n : ℝ).log) _).mul this.isBigO using 1
  · simp
  · simp_rw [Function.comp, div_mul, ← Real.sqrt_eq_rpow, Real.div_sqrt]

-- TODO(firsching): formalize any remaining remarks from the erdosproblems.com page.

end Erdos89

findings.description: The docstring says "The square grid construction, going back to Erdős and Moser". The O(n/√log n) upper bound from the square grid is due to Erdős [Er46] alone: the grid's squared distances are sums of two squares, counted by Landau–Ramanujan. Moser [Mo52] is the paper that raised the lower bound to n^{2/3}; it has nothing to do with the grid construction. The Lean statement itself is correct: I proved it equivalent to "∃ C, for all large n some n-point set has ≤ C·n/√log n distances". Only the historical attribution in the docstring is wrong, and with it the reason for listing [Mo52] among the references.
findings.source_evidence: erdosproblems.com/89 (Wayback snapshot 2026-09-03): "A √n×√n integer grid shows that this would be the best possible." Moser is not mentioned. Guth–Katz, arXiv:1011.4105, introduction: "Erdős checked that if the points are arranged in a square grid, then the number of distinct distances is ∼ N/√(log N)"; Moser [M] appears only in the list of lower-bound papers. Wikipedia, 'Erdős distinct distances problem': "In his 1946 paper, Erdős proved the estimates ... The upper bound is given by a square grid" and "g(n) = Ω(n^{2/3}) by Leo Moser in 1952". Sheffer, arXiv:1406.1949: "This was observed by Erdős, who noticed that this is an immediate corollary of [Landau–Ramanujan]". J. Pach on Gil Kalai's blog: "the first nontrivial lower bound ... due to L. Moser (1952)".
findings.suggested_fix: Reword to: "The square grid construction of Erdős [Er46] shows that n/√(log n) is the correct order if the conjecture is true ...". If [Mo52] stays in the references, cite it for the n^{2/3} lower bound instead.

reformulations.difference: The source says "every set of n distinct points in ℝ² determines ≫ n/√log n distinct distances". The Lean states `(fun n => n/√(log n)) =O[atTop] (fun n => minimalDistinctDistances ℝ² n)`, where `minimalDistinctDistances` is an `sInf` over n-point Finsets. So it uses a minimum function, `IsBigO` with the arguments swapped, and `atTop` (all large n) instead of an explicit constant.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Proved in Lean (scratch3.lean; only the standard axioms): `erdos_89 ↔ ∃ c > 0, ∀ᶠ n in atTop, ∀ A : Finset ℝ², A.card = n → c * (n / √(log n)) ≤ distinctDistances A`. The `sInf` is over a nonempty set of ℕ because ℝ² is infinite, so the minimum is attained (Nat.sInf_mem) and is ≤ the count of every n-point set (Nat.sInf_le). Both sides are nonnegative, so the Big-O constant can be taken positive and inverted. The 'for all n ≥ 2' reading is equivalent as well: minimalDistinctDistances ℝ² n ≥ 1 for n ≥ 2 (proved in Lean), so finitely many initial n are absorbed into the constant. `ℝ²` is `EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2)` with the Euclidean metric, and `offDiag` excludes the zero distance. The same argument, also proved in Lean, gives the literal forms of `erdos_89.variants.n_dvd_log_n` (Guth–Katz Theorem 1.1: ≳ N/log N) and of `erdos_89.variants.grid_upper_bound` (∃ C, for all large n some n-point set has ≤ C·n/√log n distances).

sources_consulted: https://www.erdosproblems.com/89 (Cloudflare-blocked for curl; read through Wayback snapshots)
https://arxiv.org/abs/1406.1949 (Sheffer, 'Distinct Distances: Open Problems and Current Bounds', LaTeX source)
could_not_verify: Erdos89.erdos_89.variants.grid_upper_bound (docstring attribution only; the mathematics is settled): Moser 1952 (Amer. Math. Monthly 59, 85–91) is paywalled on JSTOR and zbMATH withholds its review, so I could not rule out that the paper also discusses the grid. Every secondary source I read credits the grid bound to Erdős 1946 and Moser with the n^{2/3} lower bound. The Erdős 1946 PDF on renyi.hu is an image-only scan with no text layer, so I relied on Guth–Katz's account of what Erdős conjectured there.
review.notes:
No mathematical misformalization found.

**Declaration by declaration:**
- `erdos_89` (research open) states the $500 Erdős conjecture correctly. erdosproblems.com/89 still records it as OPEN (snapshot 2026-09-03, page last edited 23 Jan 2026, 0 proof claims), so the tag matches.
- `n_dvd_log_n` (research solved) is exactly Guth–Katz Theorem 1.1.
- `grid_upper_bound` (research solved) is Erdős's grid bound. It holds for every n, not just perfect squares, because any n-point subset of a ⌈√n⌉×⌈√n⌉ grid works; Sheffer notes this explicitly.
- `implies_n_dvd_log_n` (test) is fully proved; `#print axioms` shows only propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound.

**Boundary checks in Lean:** `minimalDistinctDistances ℝ² 0 = 0`, `minimalDistinctDistances ℝ² 1 = 0`, and `≥ 1` for n ≥ 2. The `sInf` is over a nonempty set, since ℝ² is infinite. `x/0 = 0` at n ≤ 1 is irrelevant under `atTop`.

**Remarks that are not findings:**
- The source phrases the problem as a question ("Does every set ...?"), but `erdos_89` asserts the conjectured positive answer rather than `answer(sorry) ↔ P`. CONTRIBUTING.md calls `answer(sorry)` only the "preferred style". Other open files do the same (e.g. `erdos_11`, `erdos_60`). Erdős conjectured the positive answer (Guth–Katz: "He conjectured that ... ≳ N/√(log N)"). So this is a convention question, not a mathematical defect.
- The test docstring's "strictly stronger" is loose: the theorem proves only an implication. The next sentence of the docstring describes it correctly.
- The name `n_dvd_log_n` means "n divided by log n", not divisibility. That is a naming matter only.
- The page's stronger forms are not formalized; the file marks them with a TODO. These are the single-point version (see [604]) and Erdős's Σ_x d(x) ≫ n²/√log n. A missing variant is not a misformalization.
